facts.fact: Docker packages applications into lightweight, portable containers
A Dockerfile is a text document containing commands to assemble a container image
FROM specifies the base image to build upon
RUN executes commands during image build
COPY and ADD transfer files from host to image
WORKDIR sets the working directory for subsequent instructions
EXPOSE documents which ports the container listens on
CMD specifies the default command to run when the container starts
ENTRYPOINT configures the container to run as an executable
ENV sets environment variables in the container
docker build creates an image from a Dockerfile
docker run creates and starts a container from an image
docker compose orchestrates multi-container applications with a YAML file
Volumes persist data outside the container lifecycle
Bind mounts map host directories directly into containers
Networks connect containers together and isolate them from others
Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements to optimize image size
Layer caching reuses unchanged layers to speed up builds
docker logs shows container stdout/stderr output
docker exec runs commands inside a running container
Kubernetes (K8s) orchestrates containerized applications across clusters
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage
Deployments manage replicated Pods with rolling updates and rollbacks
Services provide stable network endpoints for Pods with load balancing
ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs
Secrets store sensitive data like passwords and tokens (base64 encoded)
Ingress routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to Services
Namespaces partition cluster resources for multi-tenant isolation
PersistentVolumes provide storage that exists beyond Pod lifecycle
StatefulSets manage stateful applications with stable identities and persistent storage
DaemonSets ensure a copy of a Pod runs on all or some nodes
Jobs run Pods to completion — for batch processing
CronJobs schedule Jobs to run periodically
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales Pods based on CPU/memory or custom metrics
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — charts define, install, and upgrade apps
kubectl is the CLI for controlling Kubernetes clusters
kubectl apply creates or updates resources from YAML manifests
kubectl logs fetches container logs from Pods
kubectl exec runs commands inside Pod containers
RBAC controls access to cluster resources based on roles and bindings
CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code on every push
CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automatically releases validated code to production
GitHub Actions runs workflows triggered by GitHub events like push, PR, or schedule
Workflows are defined in .github/workflows/*.yml files
Jobs run in parallel by default — use 'needs' to create dependencies
Runners execute jobs — GitHub-hosted or self-hosted
Actions are reusable units of code for common tasks
Secrets store sensitive values encrypted and only exposed to selected actions
Matrix strategies run a job across multiple configurations (OS, version, etc.)
Artifacts persist data between jobs in a workflow
Environments group deployment targets with protection rules and secrets
GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, jobs, and runners
Jenkins is a self-hosted automation server with a plugin ecosystem
Pipeline as Code defines CI/CD in version-controlled files alongside application code
Blue-green deployment runs two identical environments, switching traffic to the new one
Canary deployment gradually shifts traffic to the new version
Rolling updates replace instances one at a time with zero downtime
Feature flags toggle functionality without deploying new code
Smoke tests verify critical functionality after deployment
Rollback strategies define how to revert to a previous version on failure
Terraform by HashiCorp manages infrastructure declaratively with HCL configuration files
Providers are plugins that interact with cloud APIs (AWS, GCP, Azure, etc.)
Resources are infrastructure components defined in Terraform configuration
terraform init downloads providers and initializes the working directory
terraform plan shows what changes will be made before applying
terraform apply creates or updates infrastructure to match configuration
terraform destroy removes all resources managed by the configuration
State files track the current state of managed infrastructure
Remote state stores state in a shared backend (S3, Terraform Cloud) for team collaboration
State locking prevents concurrent modifications that could corrupt state
Variables parameterize configurations for reuse across environments
Outputs expose resource attributes for use by other configurations
Modules encapsulate reusable groups of resources
Data sources fetch information from existing resources or external systems
Provisioners run scripts on resources after creation (use sparingly)
Workspaces manage multiple distinct state files for the same configuration
Pulumi uses general-purpose programming languages instead of HCL
Ansible automates configuration management with YAML playbooks
Idempotency ensures running the same configuration multiple times produces the same result
Drift detection identifies when actual infrastructure differs from configuration
